analysis.one_liner: Ends tax write-offs and adds a 75% excise tax on cutting old-growth redwood.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have imposed a 75% excise tax and ended all federal tax deductions for cutting old-growth redwood, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stripped federal income tax deductions — including depreciation and depletion write-offs — for any expense of cutting or hauling old-growth redwood logs, and would have added a 75% excise tax on the market value of any old-growth redwood cut, paid by whoever holds the economic interest in the timber. It defined old-growth broadly: any tract where at least 10% of the redwoods are at least 150 years old. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, which would gain the preservation of ancient redwood forests that cannot regrow on any human timescale, and taxpayers generally, who would no longer effectively subsidize old-growth logging through the tax code. Timber communities that have shifted to second-growth harvest would face less pressure on remaining old-growth stands.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public; preserved old-growth redwood forests

how_it_helps.text: Denies all income tax deductions — including depreciation and depletion allowances — for expenses of cutting old-growth redwood or transporting the unprocessed logs, ending a federal tax subsidy for logging the oldest forests.

Imposes an excise tax equal to 75% of the fair market value of any old-growth redwood cut, payable by the holder of the economic interest in the timber, and makes that tax non-deductible — economically closing off the harvest of trees more than 150 years old.

Targets the definition at genuine old growth while keeping it administrable: any tract where at least 10% of redwood trees are at least 150 years old counts, so mixed second-growth operations near ancient stands cannot avoid it.

analysis.who_pays: Holders of the economic interest in old-growth redwood timber — logging companies, timberland owners, and investors — would bear the 75% excise tax and lose every deduction. Timber workers and mill communities dependent on old-growth harvest would bear job losses, and consumers could pay more for redwood lumber.
analysis.who_pays_short: Redwood timber companies and timberland owners

drawbacks.text: A 75% excise tax plus denial of every deduction, including depreciation and depletion, is not a modest fee — it is a near-prohibition on cutting old-growth redwood accomplished through the tax code rather than through open regulation of logging, which critics would call an end run around a policy debate Congress should hold directly.

The tax falls on the holder of the economic interest, which can be a lessor, lender, or investor rather than the company doing the cutting, and the definition sweeps in any tract where just 10% of redwoods are 150 or more years old — so owners of mixed tracts could face the tax even where most trees are young.

The bill applies to all timber cut after enactment, with no transition, which would immediately devalue old-growth timber holdings and could strand owners and timber-dependent workers without compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Preserving redwood trees that are 150 or more years old has real, lasting value and cannot be undone later, and doing it by removing a tax preference costs the treasury nothing directly. But the design is blunt: a non-deductible 75% excise tax combined with the loss of all deductions functions as an outright ban on old-growth redwood harvest, with no transition for owners or workers, enacted through a short tax amendment rather than an explicit forest policy. A more considered version would pair the disincentive with compensation or a purchase program. In practice the choice the record shows is not between a blunt and a careful bill but between this bill and nothing — the committee never even considered it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: On June 19, 1991, Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill to deny deductions and impose a 75% excise tax on cutting old-growth redwood.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax law.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Redwood timber companies, timberland owners, and holders of economic interest in old-growth redwood are better off: they kept their deductions and faced no excise tax, and old-growth harvest economics were left untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Redwood timber interests kept their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny deductions for, and impose a 75% excise tax on, cutting old-growth redwood timber.

for.name: One House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Dan Rostenkowski, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats — the sponsor and a single cosponsor — were ever attached to the bill, and no votes were ever taken, so its partisan support in the full chamber was never tested.

industries.note: The 75% excise tax on the market value of cut timber, made non-deductible, plus the loss of all expense, depreciation, and depletion deductions, would have made cutting old-growth redwood uneconomic. Its interest in continuing old-growth harvest runs against the public's interest in preserving the last ancient redwood stands.

industries.industry: Timberland owners and investors holding economic interest in redwood
industries.note: The bill levies the tax directly on the holder of the economic interest in the timber, not just the operator, and its effective date is immediate, so old-growth timber holdings would lose most of their value on enactment.
